sources.title: How to Care for Aquarium Fish While on Vacation
How to Feed Fish While on Holiday: Auto Feeders, Fasting and Sitters
How to Care for Your Aquarium Fish During a Power Outage
Hướng dẫn cách cho cá ăn khi vắng nhà an toàn hiệu quả
Bí quyết chăm sóc cá cảnh trong dịp Tết

facts.fact: When nobody can look after the tank, the choice comes down to holiday food or an automatic feeder.
The usual options are not feeding at all, an automatic feeder, a pet sitter, or live food added to the tank.
Big, long-established tanks cope with long absences better than small, new or heavily stocked tanks, which are less stable.
Most fish can go 2 to 3 days without food. Newly hatched fry are the exception.
For trips of one week or less, the simplest method is not to feed at all. Aquarium Co-Op's own quarantine includes 7 days in a row with no feeding.
Healthy adult fish can go 1–3 days without food. Tetras, rasboras, guppies and corydoras handle a long weekend comfortably.
Large, carnivorous or older fish need feeding less often. Herbivores, small active fish and young fish may need food every 1 to 2 days.
Fry, newly bought fish and fish with high metabolism, such as small loaches and bettas, should be fed even on short trips.
Do not leave fish unfed if they are fry that need daily meals, sick or recovering fish, or if the trip lasts longer than a week.
Suggested plan by trip length: 1–3 days, let the fish fast; 4–7 days, use an automatic feeder; 1–3 weeks, use a reliable feeder or a fish sitter.
In a mature planted tank with established biofilm, Neocaridina and Amano shrimp need no extra food for up to two weeks.
For long trips, change 25% of the water and clean the filter about 1 week before leaving. Avoid big clean-ups, do not disturb the substrate, and leave the biological media alone.
Do maintenance about 48 hours before leaving: a partial water change, a gravel vacuum, and a filter clean if needed.
Change 30–40% of the water with conditioned tap water two days before leaving.
Do not add new fish or make big changes within 1 month before a long absence.
Check that the heater works and holds the right temperature. Put the light on a timer that follows the tank's normal day/night cycle.
Set the light timer to 6–8 hours a day, and remove dead plant leaves that could raise ammonia.
Load the automatic feeder with flakes or pellets, set the feeding times, mount it on the tank rim, and test it for several days before leaving.
Set the feeder to once a day, a little less than the usual amount, and test it for three days before leaving.
Test a holiday food block about 1 week before leaving, and give no other food during the test.
Picky fish may not accept holiday food at first, so get them used to it before you leave.
Give the sitter pre-measured food for each day in a pill box.
Frozen food cubes are cleaner than dry food and easier to portion. Label each tank with how many cubes to give.
Keep sitter instructions simple: feeding and checking for water on the floor. Ask them to visit every 2 to 3 days, and do not expect a beginner to scrape algae or change CO2 cylinders.
For evaporation, leave buckets of treated water next to each tank and mark the water level. Leave your phone number plus a backup contact, such as an experienced keeper or a local fish shop.
For picky eaters or trips over a week, add live food such as blackworms, daphnia, scuds or snails. A floating container with holes too small for the fish lets the food escape slowly.
After you come back, check the fish for injury or disease and make sure the heater works. If you were away a week or more, change some water within a few days.
After you come back, take out any food blocks or automatic feeders and return to the normal feeding schedule.
An automatic feeder must keep food away from light, air and moisture, or the food spoils. Because it is a machine, test it before you leave.
Use only dry food in a feeder. Frozen and live food spoil in the hopper.
Basic automatic feeders dispense every 12 hours. Have someone check the feeder every few days.
Feeding too much in the feeder or by hand adds waste to the tank while you are away. Give only what the trip needs.
Sitters often overfeed because they don't know aquariums. If they miss a day, they should skip it, not make up for it with extra food later.
Overfeeding by helpers kills more fish than missed meals do.
Overfeeding by a sitter is the main risk, especially in small or new tanks.
Forgetting to switch the filter back on after maintenance, and doing water changes in a rush at the last minute, are common mistakes.
Aquarium Co-Op advises against holiday feeder blocks: they break into particles that larger fish can't eat, which can cause ammonia spikes and algae blooms.
Slow-dissolving feeder blocks can cloud the water, raise pH and release food unevenly.
Tetra sells gel-based holiday food blocks, which it says feed fish for several days or weeks.

In hot, humid climates, moisture makes food clump and block the feeder. Gensou calls this a common failure in Singapore and suggests a small silica gel packet in the hopper and a model with a moisture-proof compartment.
In tropical heat, top up evaporation. A heavily stocked 120-litre tank can lose 2–3 litres a day in Singapore.
Vietnamese shops use these names: máy cho cá ăn tự động (automatic feeder), viên thức ăn tan chậm (slow-dissolving holiday food), and hộp chia thức ăn theo ngày (daily food boxes).
Vietnamese Tết guides name trùn chỉ (tubifex worms) and bo bo (daphnia/moina) as live foods that can stay alive in the tank. Máy oxy / máy sục khí is the air pump.
During a power cut, wait 1-2 hours. Then run oxygen for 1 hour every 8 hours, or every 4 hours in overstocked tanks, using an air stone or sponge filter that makes bubbles at the surface.
Aquarium Co-Op's battery air pump runs 20 hours non-stop, or 40 hours or more in power-save mode (15 seconds on, 15 seconds off).
During a power cut, switch off automatic feeders. After power comes back, wait 24 hours before feeding.

Unplug hang-on-back and canister filters during an outage and clean them before restarting, so dead bacteria and waste are not flushed into the tank. Afterwards, test ammonia and nitrite, and change water if either is above 0 ppm.
Feeding extra before leaving or after a missed day does not help the fish. Aquarium Co-Op says to skip missed portions, because extra food only adds waste.
